title: Ashoka's remorse
hookLine: the emperor conquers Kalinga, sees the slaughter, and repents (Rock Edict 13)

cards: Kings carve their victories into rock. This one carved a regret.

In a long inscription, cut by royal order where passersby could find it, a ruler who calls himself Beloved of the Gods looks back at the war that made him master of a land called Kalinga. He does not boast.
He counts: the killed, the carried away, the ones who died afterward. And then, in public stone, he says he is grieved. Scholars call it Rock Edict Thirteen.
Buddhists remember the man as Ashoka.

teach.b: First, the war, counted in stone.

Kalinga was conquered, the edict says, and great numbers of people were killed, or died, or were taken from their homes. The king puts the figures in his own inscription. Second, whose suffering weighed on him.
Not only soldiers: priests and wandering ascetics, householders who listened to their mothers and fathers, honored their teachers, and were kind to friends, relatives and servants.
They were hurt, killed, or torn from the people they loved. Even those who escaped unharmed, the edict says, grieved for friends who didn't. This weighs on the king heavily.
Third, the turn. After Kalinga, his devotion to dhamma grew: to the good way of living, to care, to restraint.
He calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest, and asks his sons and grandsons not to seek new conquests, or, if they must conquer, to choose patience and light punishment.
Fourth, the regret made public. He could have kept it in his heart; he put it where strangers would read it. A Buddhist sutta sits beside it.
King Ajatasattu confesses to the Buddha that he killed his own father. The Buddha doesn't excuse it.
He says that seeing a wrong as a wrong, owning it, and restraining yourself after is growth in the discipline of the noble ones. Regret isn't the end of the story; it's where the turning starts.
The edict doesn't bring back anyone from Kalinga, and doesn't pretend to. It just refuses to call the war glorious.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Ashoka after Kalinga as an example of a ruler who turned from conquest to dhamma, and the edict is read today as a public act of regret.

o: a curse the defeated people laid on the emperor
a conqueror's grief over his war, carved in stone
a king's fear of losing the throne he had won

games.q: the conqueror repents: tap the pairs.
p: the title the king uses for himself
what the edict calls the best conquest
a king who confessed to the Buddha

s: Ashoka left the war out of his inscriptions
the edict names Kalinga and counts the killed and the carried away, in public stone.
the edict grieves for ordinary people, not only soldiers
it names priests, ascetics and householders who were hurt, killed or torn from those they loved.
the edict urges his descendants to win new lands
it asks them not to seek new conquests, and to prefer patience and light punishment if they do.

games.q: you're an emperor. you've won the war and the land is yours, but the cost in lives was terrible. what do you carve in stone?
o: the cost of the war, your grief, and a new aim.
nothing. the less said, the better.
games.why: the edict counts the cost, says the king is grieved, and calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you did that you'd take back, not the worst thing in your life, just one real one, and look at it the way the edict looks at Kalinga: what happened, and who it touched.
No excuses, and no beating yourself up either. Then ask quietly what restraint or small amends might follow, and let the question rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Ashoka's remorse. A conqueror who looked at what his war had cost, said so in stone, and turned toward dhamma.

orig.note: Prakrit: beloved of the gods, the title Ashoka uses for himself in the edicts.

carryVoice: Your line: the conqueror repents. Seeing a wrong as a wrong is where the turning starts. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.
